name: Pompeian Red
lede: Pompeian red is a muted brick red named for the walls of Pompeii, and in the pigment trade it was a name for a natural iron-oxide red also sold as Venetian or Indian red.

sections.title: A name for the walls of Pompeii
sections.body:
St Clair's glossary of color names lists Pompeian red as a dark brick red, taking its name from houses that archaeologists dug out at Pompeii [1]. Paterson's dictionary defines it as the red found in the frescoes of Pompeii and sends the reader to Venetian red [2].

In the pigment trade the name drifted onto a plain oxide red. Venetian red is an orange-red or reddish-brown natural iron oxide, sold under many regional names, including Venice, Indian, Spanish, Pompeian and Persian red [3][4]. Heaton in 1928 listed Pompeian red as a current name for a light Indian red, which he defined as a highly calcined iron oxide [5]. The books therefore disagree on how dark it is: a dark brick red in one, a light red in another [1][5].

sections.title: With dark greens, in the Empire
sections.body: In France in the First Empire, greens were still dark and were set beside Pompeian reds or crimsons and bright gold [6]. Pastoureau adds that it is a myth that Napoleon started this "Empire green" fashion [6].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: Our swatch is a library color with three early sources: the ISCC-NBS system of 1955, Ridgway's *Color Standards* of 1912 and Maerz and Paul of 1930 [7]. It is a moderate red, 3.9 units from the ISCC-NBS center [7]. Its closest relatives in the earth reds are [[venetian-red]], [[indian-red]], [[brick-red]] and [[terracotta]] [7].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, Pompeian red appears in 248, 1.04 per cent, and is more common than 70 per cent of the named colors [8]. It peaks in the 1400s, in 2.3 per cent of 945 paintings, about 2.2 times what the same museums would predict [8]. It most often plays an accent (81 per cent of 196 works measured) [8]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [8]. The term itself appears in Google Books from about 1860 and peaks around 1920 [9].

origin.named_after: Pompeii, from the red walls found there

openers: In the paint trade, Pompeian red could mean the same oxide red as Venetian red or Indian red.
